name: Half-Day Strategy Workshop Facilitation Deck
description: A rigorous half-day strategy workshop facilitation system in warm white, black, and deep red for contracting with the room, grounding debate in shared facts, structuring breakout canvases, scoring options, naming owners, and closing with dated first moves.
style_guide:
# Half-Day Strategy Workshop Facilitation Deck

## Design intent

Create a working deck that helps a facilitator move 12–20 leaders through a demanding four-hour strategy session and leave with a small number of chosen priorities, one accountable owner for each, an immediate first move, a check-in date, and a clearly stated kill criterion. The deck is a room instrument, not a speech. It must make time, rules, evidence, questions, canvases, scoring, voting, and commitments visible enough that participants can work without waiting for verbal instructions.

The visual identity uses warm white, institutional black, and decisive deep red. High-contrast editorial serif headlines make each act feel consequential. Condensed mono labels expose timing, sequence, roles, and facilitation cues. Red marks active debate, boundaries, vote dots, ownership, and irreversible decisions; black creates the stage for rules, synthesis, and commitment.

Preview images define visual and facilitation patterns only. Do not reuse preview organizations, business context, facilitator, date, objectives, agenda times, rules, metrics, strategic options, votes, people, actions, or conclusions. Rebuild the session from the current workshop brief and keep all unresolved choices editable.

## Core visual signature

- Treat the six-page deck as five timed acts: frame, establish facts, break out, evaluate, and commit.
- Use warm-white pages with a narrow red top rail and a black footer rail. Full black panels hold rules, synthesis, selected options, or commitment prompts.
- Use large editorial serif statements that can be read from the back of a room. Follow each with a red italic operating instruction.
- Place a visible timer block at upper right on every working page.
- Use condensed mono labels for act number, start and finish time, section identifier, table role, delivery format, facilitator note, and page counter.
- Design every canvas to be written on, printed, projected, or recreated in a shared board. Empty space is functional.

## Canvas, grid, and spacing

- Author on a fixed 1920 × 1080, 16:9 canvas.
- Keep working content within 80 px side margins and 34–60 px top margins. Reserve 28–36 px for the top red rail and 28–40 px for the black footer band.
- Use a 12-column grid with 20–24 px gutters. Align timer, act labels, tables, canvases, matrices, and commitment rows to stable anchors.
- Reserve 170–230 px for act label, headline, red facilitation sentence, and timer.
- Use 24–36 px between major working regions and 12–20 px inside forms, tables, and prompt cards.
- Prefer sharp rectangles, 1–2 px rules, and no shadow. This is a printed working-paper language, not a software dashboard.
- Keep workshop body text at 18–23 px, labels at 12–16 px, prompt text at 25–34 px, and headlines at 54–82 px.

## Color system

### Primary palette

- Warm paper white: #F4F3EF. Default canvas, writable area, evidence field, and participant handout surface.
- Institutional black: #1B1B1A. Primary type, rules panel, timer, table header, selected-option field, and footer.
- Decision red: #B31D25. Act labels, top rail, italic instruction, option markers, vote dots, owners, alerts, and commitment emphasis.
- Clean white: #FFFFFF. Cards and reverse text within dark panels.
- Fine rule gray: #BEBDB8. Canvas borders, axes, separators, and empty writing guides.
- Soft cream: #E7E2D2. Break or neutral agenda state and gentle annotation.

### Semantic exceptions

- Decision green: #287E52 only for a verified committed or completed action where the workshop process requires it.
- Timing amber: #B87916 only for a time warning or unresolved near-term dependency.
- Exception colors require explicit text and should appear rarely; they are not primary preset colors.
- Red does not automatically mean failure. In this system it means active, contested, selected, or accountable. Written labels carry the semantic state.

## Typography

- Use Source Serif 4, Georgia, or another authoritative editorial serif for page headlines, questions, commitments, synthesis, and reflection prompts.
- Use Arial Narrow, IBM Plex Sans Condensed, or another condensed sans/mono for act labels, times, roles, table headings, instructions, footer notes, and page numbers.
- Use Inter, Arial, or a neutral sans serif for dense data, explanatory annotations, chart labels, and form instructions where serif would slow scanning.
- Italic serif in red may express one facilitation instruction or tension beneath the headline.
- Cover and act headlines may be 60–88 px; canvas questions 30–42 px; body text 18–23 px; mono operational labels 12–16 px with generous tracking.
- Keep participant-facing questions in sentence case. Use all caps only for short operational metadata.
- Do not use multiple decorative serif families. Consistency is essential when pages are read quickly under time pressure.

## Persistent frame and room controls

- Place act number, exact time window, and act purpose at upper left.
- Place a high-contrast timer box at upper right with duration and, when useful, start and close time.
- Carry a facilitator-only note in the black footer band: what to read, when to pause, where to move, and how to intervene.
- Add a two-digit page counter and page purpose at lower right.
- Use stable terms: objective, rule, shared fact, question, canvas, evidence, deliverable, criterion, score, vote, priority, owner, first move, check-in, kill criterion.
- Keep agenda times, timer durations, and footer instructions synchronized. A mismatch undermines facilitation.

## Page archetypes

### Workshop cover and session context

State workshop purpose, format, participant range, total duration, number of acts, expected outputs, facilitator, sponsor, business unit, session date, location or channel, and version. Phrase the outcome as an artifact the room will leave with. Do not promise consensus if the governance model only requires a decision owner.

### Objectives, rules, and agenda

List no more than three concrete workshop outputs. Establish three to five behavioral rules and secure explicit agreement. Show the run of show with start time, segment title, output, duration, break, and hard close. Name decision rights: who participates, who recommends, who decides, and how dissent is recorded.

### Current-state review and shared facts

Use a small set of verified facts to establish the strategic problem before debate. Present four to six metrics, one or two trends, a one-sentence synthesis, and two to four facts the room will not relitigate. Include source, period, definition, and evidence cutoff. End with one discussion prompt that translates evidence into strategic implication.

### Breakout questions and working canvases

Assign each table one sharply bounded question and a fillable canvas. State host, scribe, evidence standard, deliverable format, report-out time, and exact schedule. Design canvases for specific outputs such as causes plus evidence, segment plus moat, or work to stop plus stakeholder communication. The facilitator rescues process but does not steer content.

### Impact-feasibility scoring and vote

Place candidate options on an impact-feasibility matrix using definitions the room can defend. Show the scoring rubric, criterion weights, placement rationale, vote rule, conflicts or abstentions, and selected options. Separate score from vote: scoring structures judgment; voting records preference or decision according to the agreed governance.

### Commitments, owners, and close

Turn selected priorities into a commitment board with accountable owner, first action, due date, 30-day review, success measure, dependency, and kill criterion. Ask short closing-reflection questions that surface confidence, dissent, risk, and personal commitment. End on the exact follow-up mechanism, not a generic thank-you page.

## Facilitation and evidence integrity

- Preview content is not reusable. Never copy the preview company, metrics, options, people, dates, votes, agenda, actions, or strategic conclusion.
- Distinguish verified fact, participant observation, hypothesis, option, score, vote, facilitator synthesis, sponsor decision, and committed action.
- Never invent revenue, margin, retention, win rate, market share, headcount, customer evidence, option scores, votes, owners, or commitments.
- Shared facts require source, definition, period, and cutoff. If participants dispute the data, record the issue and decide whether it blocks the session.
- Do not label an interpretation as a fact. Keep “what the data says” separate from “what it may mean.”
- Workshop objectives must be achievable within the scheduled time and decision authority. Do not promise a final strategy when the session can only produce hypotheses or recommendations.
- Rules of engagement require sponsor support and should match the culture and power dynamics of the room. Do not copy confrontational language mechanically.
- Breakout questions must be mutually distinct, evidence-seeking, and answerable. Each needs a concrete deliverable.
- Scoring criteria must be defined before options are rated. Show scale, weights, evidence basis, and who scored.
- Dot voting is not automatically a decision. State whether it is input, prioritization, recommendation, or binding choice.
- Record abstentions, conflicts, unresolved dissent, minority view, and conditions where governance requires them.
- Every priority needs one accountable owner, not a committee. Contributors and consulted parties may be listed separately.
- A first move must be observable and dated. “Socialize,” “align,” or “explore” is insufficient without an artifact and audience.
- A kill criterion needs a measurable condition, time window, decision owner, and consequence. Avoid arbitrary thresholds.
- Participant names, performance comments, sensitive strategy, customer details, and confidential metrics require appropriate handling and distribution.
- For remote or hybrid workshops, include tool access, backup channel, breakout logistics, facilitation roles, and how votes are authenticated.

## Canvas, chart, and interaction rules

- Use writable boxes, dotted guides, clear columns, and generous blank space. Slides should survive printing in grayscale.
- Use a simple line chart, bar chart, or metric card only when it grounds the discussion. Avoid building a decorative dashboard.
- Label axes and matrix quadrants in plain language. Define “impact” and “feasibility” for the current organization and horizon.
- Keep option names short but attach a one-sentence definition and evidence note.
- Use numbered red circles or dots to connect options across the matrix, score table, selection list, and commitment board.
- Place participant instructions on the page and facilitator-only behavior in the footer.
- Do not use animations that hide instructions from printed or asynchronous copies.
- If a collaborative whiteboard is used, mirror the slide IDs and fields so capture and synthesis remain traceable.

## Timing and room choreography

- Build a complete run of show with hard starts, hard stops, transitions, break, report-outs, voting, commitment, and close.
- Keep a 5–10 percent facilitation buffer or explicitly identify which discussion can be shortened.
- Begin each act by stating outcome, method, evidence standard, deliverable, and time.
- Use silent reading or writing before open debate when hierarchy may suppress independent thought.
- During breakout, visit groups at planned intervals and ask process questions rather than supplying answers.
- Timebox report-outs equally. Capture verbatim outputs before synthesizing.
- Before voting, clarify criteria, decision right, number of votes, self-voting rule, and what happens to unselected options.
- Before close, ask each owner to confirm commitment aloud and calendar the first review.

## Content rules

- The room should know at all times: where we are, what question we are answering, what evidence counts, what artifact is due, and how much time remains.
- Use one dominant question or canvas per page.
- Limit shared facts to what changes the choice. Send detailed analysis as a pre-read or appendix.
- Limit candidate options to six to eight, selected priorities to three or four, and closing prompts to three.
- Phrase questions to force specificity: what changed, why now, where do we win, what stops, what evidence would change our mind, who owns the first move.
- Capture words in the room before polishing them. Preserve dissent and uncertainty.
- Keep facilitation language direct, humane, and culturally appropriate.

## Allowed variation

- Adapt the five acts to portfolio strategy, market entry, operating model, transformation, product direction, nonprofit priorities, or risk response.
- Adjust timing for three- or five-hour sessions, but recalculate every act and preserve a hard close.
- Use black panels for rules, synthesis, selected options, or commitments. Keep most writable surfaces warm white.
- Replace the impact-feasibility matrix with value-risk, urgency-confidence, desirability-viability, or another defensible decision model.
- Use red as the active thread in rails, numbers, dots, italics, and ownership markers without treating all red items as negative.

## Avoid

- Do not reuse preview metrics, strategic options, participant names, scores, votes, commitments, dates, or business conclusions.
- Do not let the deck become a lecture; build pages around room work and explicit outputs.
- Do not ask broad questions that produce slogans instead of evidence.
- Do not use dot voting as a substitute for decision rights or executive accountability.
- Do not hide disagreement, unresolved data quality, abstentions, or sponsor overrides.
- Do not assign group ownership where one accountable person is required.
- Do not end without first actions, due dates, review dates, and kill criteria.
- Do not use soft decorative gradients, oversized rounded cards, stock teamwork photography, emoji, clip art, tiny footnotes, or software-dashboard chrome.
- Do not let timer boxes, agenda durations, and actual facilitation notes contradict one another.
